case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old man presented with left cervical and left inguinal masses. He reported intermittent itching and night sweats for 2 years. He denied fever, weight loss, shortness of breath, rashes, diarrhea, and neurological symptoms. On a preemployment evaluation, the patient was told he had a high white blood cell count 2 years ago. On examination, there was left cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy and no other organomegaly. Complete blood cell count and peripheral blood smear showed marked leukocytosis, with a white blood cell count of 22 340/μL, an absolute neutrophil count of 5360/μL, and 55% eosinophils with an absolute eosinophil count of 12 290/μL (to convert all to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Vitamin B12was markedly elevated at more than 4000 pg/mL (to convert to pmol/L, multiply by 0.7378). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 5 mm/h. Lactate dehydrogenase was 180 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 81 U/L (to convert both to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Evaluations for HIV and hepatitis B and C were all negative. Serum creatinine was 0.76 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4); alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were 11 U/L and 9.9 U/L, respectively (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167); and total bilirubin was 0.35 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104). Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%. Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan showed a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm and a left inguinal lymph node of 3.1 × 2.3 cm with an standardized uptake value max of 5.7 (Figure, A). Left inguinal lymph node biopsy showed partial involvement by atypical cells with high proliferation index (Ki-67 >95%) that were positive for CD3, CD4, CD8,BCL2, and TDT, suggestive of T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (Figure, B).

case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.caption: A, Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan of the head and neck at presentation showing a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm (arrowhead). B, Lymph node biopsy immunohistochemical stain with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. The inset shows interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization forFIP1L1::PDGFRArearrangement (positive). case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.caption: A, Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan of the head and neck at presentation showing a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm (arrowhead). B, Lymph node biopsy immunohistochemical stain with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. The inset shows interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization forFIP1L1::PDGFRArearrangement (positive). C, PET/CT 12 weeks after treatment initiation.
case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Currently reachable stages (Hitchcock ordering rules): CONSIDER, INFORM, PROPOSE, RECOMMEND, REVISE
You MUST pick a stage from this list.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 31-year-old man presented with left cervical and left inguinal masses. He reported intermittent itching and night sweats for 2 years. He denied fever, weight loss, shortness of breath, rashes, diarrhea, and neurological symptoms. On a preemployment evaluation, the patient was told he had a high white blood cell count 2 years ago. On examination, there was left cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy and no other organomegaly. Complete blood cell count and peripheral blood smear showed marked leukocytosis, with a white blood cell count of 22 340/μL, an absolute neutrophil count of 5360/μL, and 55% eosinophils with an absolute eosinophil count of 12 290/μL (to convert all to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Vitamin B12was markedly elevated at more than 4000 pg/mL (to convert to pmol/L, multiply by 0.7378). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 5 mm/h. Lactate dehydrogenase was 180 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 81 U/L (to convert both to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Evaluations for HIV and hepatitis B and C were all negative. Serum creatinine was 0.76 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4); alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were 11 U/L and 9.9 U/L, respectively (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167); and total bilirubin was 0.35 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104). Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%. Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan showed a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm and a left inguinal lymph node of 3.1 × 2.3 cm with an standardized uptake value max of 5.7 (Figure, A). Left inguinal lymph node biopsy showed partial involvement by atypical cells with high proliferation index (Ki-67 >95%) that were positive for CD3, CD4, CD8,BCL2, and TDT, suggestive of T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (Figure, B).

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 6.4. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."

[Clinical case]
A 31-year-old man presented with left cervical and left inguinal masses. He reported intermittent itching and night sweats for 2 years. He denied fever, weight loss, shortness of breath, rashes, diarrhea, and neurological symptoms. On a preemployment evaluation, the patient was told he had a high white blood cell count 2 years ago. On examination, there was left cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy and no other organomegaly. Complete blood cell count and peripheral blood smear showed marked leukocytosis, with a white blood cell count of 22 340/μL, an absolute neutrophil count of 5360/μL, and 55% eosinophils with an absolute eosinophil count of 12 290/μL (to convert all to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Vitamin B12was markedly elevated at more than 4000 pg/mL (to convert to pmol/L, multiply by 0.7378). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 5 mm/h. Lactate dehydrogenase was 180 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 81 U/L (to convert both to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Evaluations for HIV and hepatitis B and C were all negative. Serum creatinine was 0.76 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4); alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were 11 U/L and 9.9 U/L, respectively (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167); and total bilirubin was 0.35 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104). Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%. Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan showed a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm and a left inguinal lymph node of 3.1 × 2.3 cm with an standardized uptake value max of 5.7 (Figure, A). Left inguinal lymph node biopsy showed partial involvement by atypical cells with high proliferation index (Ki-67 >95%) that were positive for CD3, CD4, CD8,BCL2, and TDT, suggestive of T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (Figure, B).

Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions, as indicated by the elevated eosinophil count and the presence of the FIP1L1::PDGFRA rearrangement. [AI Assistant]: You mentioned the presence of the FIP1L1::PDGFRA rearrangement. Could you clarify what evidence in the case leads you to that specific genetic finding? I'm interested in understanding the basis for that interpretation.
[Doctor]: The FIP1L1::PDGFRA rearrangement is often associated with myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms that present with eosinophilia, which fits this patient's profile. While the case doesn't explicitly mention genetic testing performed, the combination of marked eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy, and a hypercellular marrow with myeloid hyperplasia raises a strong suspicion for this diagnosis. Additionally, the presence of atypical cells with a high proliferation index from the lymph node biopsy suggests an underlying neoplastic process consistent with tyrosine kinase gene fusions. I believe this is the most likely explanation for his clinical presentation and laboratory findings.
[AI Assistant]: Let's evaluate this suspicion against the definitive pathology result. While the clinical features fit a myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia, the lymph node biopsy shows a definitive diagnosis of T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (T-ALL/LBL) with a specific immunophenotype. This conclusive evidence of a T-cell malignancy takes precedence over a suspected reactive or associated myeloid phenomenon.
[Doctor]: While the lymph node biopsy indeed suggests T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia, I still believe that the eosinophilia and the hypercellular marrow with myeloid features point toward an underlying myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm. I would advocate for additional testing to confirm the genetic basis of these findings before fully committing to a diagnosis of T-ALL.
[AI Assistant]: I agree that investigating the eosinophilia is essential. Given the confirmed T-ALL, a logical next step is to perform genetic testing on the T-ALL cells or the marrow for associated driver mutations, such as PDGFRA/B, FGFR1, or JAK2, which could explain the paraneoplastic eosinophilia within the context of this T-cell malignancy, rather than pursuing a separate primary myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm.

However, I remain concerned that the presence of marked eosinophilia and the specific profile of the marrow findings might indicate an underlying myeloid process. While testing for mutations in T-ALL is certainly important, I believe we should not overlook the possibility of a primary myeloid neoplasm that could account for the eosinophilia. [AI Assistant]: I understand your desire for a comprehensive genetic workup. case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old man presented with left cervical and left inguinal masses. He reported intermittent itching and night sweats for 2 years. He denied fever, weight loss, shortness of breath, rashes, diarrhea, and neurological symptoms. On a preemployment evaluation, the patient was told he had a high white blood cell count 2 years ago. On examination, there was left cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy and no other organomegaly. Complete blood cell count and peripheral blood smear showed marked leukocytosis, with a white blood cell count of 22 340/μL, an absolute neutrophil count of 5360/μL, and 55% eosinophils with an absolute eosinophil count of 12 290/μL (to convert all to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). Vitamin B12was markedly elevated at more than 4000 pg/mL (to convert to pmol/L, multiply by 0.7378). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 5 mm/h. Lactate dehydrogenase was 180 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 81 U/L (to convert both to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Evaluations for HIV and hepatitis B and C were all negative. Serum creatinine was 0.76 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4); alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were 11 U/L and 9.9 U/L, respectively (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167); and total bilirubin was 0.35 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104). Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%. Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan showed a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm and a left inguinal lymph node of 3.1 × 2.3 cm with an standardized uptake value max of 5.7 (Figure, A). Left inguinal lymph node biopsy showed partial involvement by atypical cells with high proliferation index (Ki-67 >95%) that were positive for CD3, CD4, CD8,BCL2, and TDT, suggestive of T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (Figure, B).

case_info.explanation: D. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions The differential diagnoses in young men with eosinophilia and a neck mass can be wide. The typical presentation of Kimura disease is a painless, unilateral swelling of cervical lymph nodes in young adult male patients with peripheral blood eosinophilia and elevated immunoglobulin E levels. Histological evaluation, however, would show hyperplastic reactive follicles with eosinophilic infiltrates in a background of polymorphous inflammatory cells, a picture inconsistent with the presented case. Although Hodgkin lymphoma can present with eosinophilia and neck mass in young adults, the biopsy was inconsistent with the typical morphology of Reed-Sternberg cells in the background of nonneoplastic inflammatory cells. The diagnosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia is reasonable given the morphology from lymph node biopsy; however, in the diagnosis hierarchy, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions (MLN-TK) would supersede other myeloid and lymphoid cancers.1 In the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours, MLN-TK refers toBCR::ABL1–negative myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with gene rearrangements leading to an activated tyrosine-kinase domain that results in cell-signaling dysregulation.1This includesPDGFRA,PDGFRB,FGFR1,JAK2, andFLT3rearrangements, in addition toETV6::ABL1,ETV6::FGFR2,ETV6::LYN,ETV6::NTRK3,RANBP2::ALK,BCR::RET, andFGFR1OP::RETfusions.1An increase in vitamin B12is often found in patients withPDGFRAandPDGFRBdisease.2,3Most patients are male with chronic myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia; however, patients rarely present with acute myeloid or T-cell leukemia or extramedullary disease.2 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRA(4q12) fusion in 91% of nuclei, while karyotype was normal (46, XY in 18 cells), as a cryptic loss of theCHIC2gene causes this fusion. Next, generation sequencing panel for myeloid neoplasms was negative for variants in targeted regions of the genes commonly involved in myeloid neoplasms. Combining imatinib with chemotherapy is acceptable in patients with acute leukemia or extramedullary diseases, although monotherapy with imatinib has shown promising results.4The patient was concerned about fertility, as he and his partner were starting a family, and decided to avoid chemotherapy. The patient was concomitantly initiated on 1 mg/kg of prednisone for 7 days and imatinib at 600 mg daily. The eosinophil counts normalized after 2 days, and bone marrow evaluation after 4 weeks showed resolution of eosinophilic infiltration; however, FISH results were 3% positive forFIP1L1::PDGFRAfusion. Repeat bone marrow evaluation after 8 weeks showed complete resolution of the FISH abnormality, and the imatinib dose was reduced to 400 mg daily. Although studies have confirmed deep and durable remission with a starting dose of imatinib, 100 mg, we elected to start with a high dose given the patient’s young age and blastic presentation.5,6Follow-up positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan 12 weeks after initiation of imatinib was consistent with complete metabolic remission (Figure,C). Complete hematological remission is achieved in more than 95% of patients with imatinib and is typically seen early (within weeks of treatment initiation). Cytogenetic/molecular response can be achieved within 3 to 6 months of treatment initiation.7In patients who achieved molecular remission, the imatinib dose can be reduced to 100 thrice weekly or weekly.8Treatment-free remission as the experience with chronic myeloid leukemia has been tried, although with limited experience. The success rate is around 60%, with most patients relapsing within the first 10 months. Reinitiating of imatinib restores hematological remission in almost all patients.9,10 The current patient was in complete remission 12 months from his treatment and receiving imatinib. Evaluating patients suspected of MLN-TK is critical, as treatment and prognosis may drastically change.
